conversation.content: Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us see how mood, anxiety, and sleep are going for new moms. Anything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and we’ll go at whatever pace feels comfortable. Ready to start? First, how have you been enjoying things these past seven days—little moments with the baby, a favorite show, even a good cup of coffee?

Hi Sarah. Yeah, I’ve still been enjoying things. When the baby gives me one of those sleepy milk-drunk smiles, it makes me smile right back. And I caught up on my favorite show during a late feeding last night—still felt like a little treat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—my partner did that silly dance with the burp cloth yesterday and I cracked up.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to stuff—like tomorrow I’m planning to take the baby on a short walk to the park. It’s small, but it feels nice to have that to aim for.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
I really haven’t been beating myself up. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed him, I just figure it’s normal baby stuff, not something I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I do get a little anxious sometimes—like I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay when he’s napping in the bassinet. It’s not constant, just pops in and then I check on him and feel fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any sudden scares or panic feelings—just the normal new-mom nerves when I hear him hiccup in the middle of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, sure—like yesterday when he wanted to cluster-feed right when I’d finally sat down to eat my own lunch. For a minute I felt a bit overwhelmed, but it passed once I got him settled and scarfed my sandwich one-handed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Not at all—once my head hits the pillow, I’m out pretty quickly. The baby gives me one good four-hour stretch most nights, so I feel lucky there.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt really sad or miserable—maybe just a little tired or “blah” on the days when the feedings run together, but it lifts once I shower or step outside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t had any of those tearful spells. Maybe a quick tear when I yawn really big at 3 a.m., but it’s not from feeling unhappy—just exhaustion.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind at all.

It sounds as though you are settling into new parenthood with flashes of joy and realistic expectations. You still laugh with your partner, look forward to small outings, and take normal baby moments in stride, even when cluster-feeding interrupts lunch. You shared brief worries about the baby's breathing, yet these pass quickly after a quick check, and you report no persistent sadness, guilt, or thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 4, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>"Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> symptoms. Scores of 0 on Q1-Q3, Q5, Q7, Q9, Q10 indicate preserved enjoyment, no guilt, no panic, no sleep-mood link, no tearfulness, and no self-harm thoughts. Q4 score 2 reflects mild <sym>anxiety</sym> but without persistence or impairment. Q6 score 1 captures situational stress, not pervasive hopelessness. Total 4 falls well below the 8-point threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. She therefore does not meet screening criteria for further diagnostic evaluation at this time. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine pediatric and postpartum visits
2. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding when brief worries arise
3. Re-screen EPDS at 6-week postpartum check or sooner if mood drops
4. Encourage partner support and brief self-care daily
5. Return promptly if intrusive worries intensify, low mood persists, or functioning declines
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner report available)

A. Positive endorsements (within-normal range)  
• Maintains capacity for enjoyment/humor and future-oriented planning  
• Denies persistent low mood, excessive guilt, tearfulness, sleep-mood link, or self-harm ideation  

B. Subthreshold / monitoring indicators  
• Occasional intrusive worry about infant safety (Q4) – resolves quickly with checking  
• Transient feeling “overwhelmed” with cluster-feeding (Q6) – situational, brief, no impairment noted  

C. Risk factors / red flags – none identified  
• No sustained anhedonia, guilt, panic, or suicidal thoughts reported  

Screening impression:  
Responses do not indicate clinically significant depressive or anxiety symptoms at this time. Routine postpartum follow-up recommended; return sooner if mood worsens, worries intensify, or functioning declines.
